_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Working Lands & Industry' — forestry, ranching, mining, and agriculture, the resource economy that defines the Cariboo and rural BC.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-14: geopolitical and war news with no resource-economy connection; consumer tech and gadget reviews; wildlife content with no agricultural or working-lands relevance; crime and judicial news unrelated to resource industries; financial market and stock ticker stories.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Trade-press journalism counts fully: equipment, markets, and operations coverage is a real fit, not a near-zero. A BC tie raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent working-lands journalism. BC/Cariboo forestry, ranching, mining, and agriculture stories land here (mill closures, beetle kill, BCTS, Cariboo ranchers and water rights, local mine operations, Cariboo Cattlemen) — and so does outstanding national trade reporting with real operational or economic depth.
- 55-79: Solid resource-economy journalism anywhere in Canada or beyond — Western Producer or Northern Miner-style coverage of farm machinery, harvest technology, livestock and commodity markets, mining operations and exploration, AgTech and precision agriculture, silviculture, sawmills, drone survey work, mine automation, and labour/workforce stories in these industries. Most genuine trade journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Broader agriculture, forestry, or mining news with clear working-lands relevance but thin reporting — general farm economics, international resource-industry briefs, climate impacts on working lands.
- 15-29: Tangential mentions — a business, policy, or science story that touches forestry/agriculture/mining in passing, or Cariboo civic news unrelated to working lands.

ANCHORS: 'Williams Lake sawmill cuts second shift as beetle-kill supply dwindles' → 95. 'New John Deere baler cuts hay-drying time by a third' → 70. 'Cattle futures slip on weaker export demand' → 60. 'Global copper prices hit two-year high' → 40.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] The adult brain can repair itself better than scientists thought
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The adult brain may be far better at repairing itself than scientists once believed. In mice, researchers discovered a special group of support cells called astrocytes that respond to damaged brain tissue by rebuilding lost cellular networks. Rather than simply moving into the injured area, these cells perform a remarkable maneuver: they create new nuclei and send them traveling through long cellular extensions to repopulate damaged regions.

items.title: [Fast Company] More than half of workers would take a pay cut for job security
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Employees in 2026 are seriously worried about how unstable their jobs may be. So worried, in fact, that more than half say they’d willingly swap part of their paycheck for greater job security.

According to a new survey from Monster, which recently polled 1,020 U.S. employees across a range of industries, job security is of the utmost importance to workers today. While earning a decent living is massively important, as the cost of living soars, most workers would still trade a chunk of their salary for the promise of continued work. A whopping 54% of those surveyed said they’d take a pay cut for greater job stability. 

Exactly how large of a pay cut workers would trade varied. The survey found that more than a quarter (28%) would accept a salary reduction of at least 5%, including 11% who said they’d take a salary reduction of 10% to know their job was secure.

Additionally, workers would also trade other massively important benefits to know their job was safe, too. Twenty-six percent said they’d take reduced bonuses or incentives, as well as workplace perks or benefits. Even the almighty flexibility was on the table, with 23% saying they’d even give up the option to work remotely. Meanwhile, 17% said they’d willingly pay higher health insurance costs.

Not everyone values job security over every other workplace benefit, however. 

Thirty-nine percent say they wouldn’t give up their salary, remote work, their bonuses, or anything at all to ensure their job was safe. Still, the large majority (61%) feel that holding onto their job is the most important offering on the table, as that percentage of workers would give up at least one workplace incentive to stay employed.

The latest stats show just how important job security is to Americans today. And given recent job loss data, the numbers add up. 

A recent Labor Department report showed that U.S. employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs last month. After Labor Department revisions, there were 103,000 jobs taken off payrolls in May and June. And while unemployment fell to 4.1%, it only happened because 264,000 Americans stopped looking for work altogether.

Still, job insecurity is hardly a new concern for Americans. Last year, the American Psychological Association’s 2025 Work in America survey found that more than half of American workers (54%) said concerns about their workplace stability had a “significant impact” on how stressed they were. 

“When people feel their jobs are at risk, it creates a sense of uncertainty that can affect every aspect of their lives,” Dr. Arthur C. Evans Jr., APA’s chief executive officer, said in a news release at the time.

Evans continued: “This cultural moment is threatening workers’ sense of stability, control and ability to meet their basic needs. And feelings of insecurity at work and poor mental health can amplify each other in a vicious cycle.”

items.title: [ArchDaily] Beyond the Handmade Aesthetic: Why Craft Needs New Construction Economies
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

There has never been a more celebrated moment for craftsmanship in architecture. Across magazines, awards, and international exhibitions, handmade brick, lime plaster, carved stone, woven bamboo, and rammed earth have re-emerged as symbols of environmental responsibility, cultural continuity, and architectural authenticity. Beyond these carefully documented projects lies another reality. The overwhelming majority of buildings constructed today, from apartment blocks and office towers to public housing and commercial developments, continue to rely on industrialized systems that leave little room for skilled artisans. Craft has become increasingly visible at the very moment it has become increasingly uncommon. In countries such as India, the contrast is difficult to ignore. Centuries-old building traditions continue alongside one of the world's fastest-growing construction industries. To reframe the question of why craftsmanship is returning, perhaps the intrigue is why it now appears primarily where construction budgets, timelines, and clients can afford it.
